forecasts.label: Capital financing requirement
forecasts.note: Restated at each quarterly return. The Q4 restatement comes from the annual return itself, so it lands on the outturn by construction — the interesting movement is Q1 to Q3.

forecasts.label: Interest payable
forecasts.note: The council's own full-year forecast, restated at each quarterly return.

forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)
forecasts.note: The full-year forecast of net current expenditure — the running cost of services — restated each quarter against the same measure at outturn.

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

news_drafts.headline: Ribble Valley reports £36,047 net overspend at half-year after excluding £459,187 of unspent grants
news_drafts.lead:
Ribble Valley Council's Policy and Finance Committee was told that its half-year day-to-day spending for 2026/27 stands at a net overspend of £36,047, once £459,187 of grants not yet spent is excluded. The revenue monitoring paper names five grants in that adjustment: the Crisis and Resilience Fund, Renters Rights, Building Safety Levy, Asylum Dispersal and Homelessness Grant. It says: "Excluding these grants gives an adjusted adverse variance of £36,047."

The same papers show a £28,250 overspend on internal audit. The full-year budget is £94,860 and actual spending, including commitments to the end of the period, is £123,110. The service was outsourced after recruitment to vacant posts was unsuccessful, as the committee approved in March 2026. The paper says the cost is for work by the accountancy firm MIAA "during 2026/27 in respect of the 2025/26 financial year". It will be met from earmarked reserves, set aside last year from the vacant internal audit posts.

The capital monitoring paper shows a £130,400 overspend on the purchase of an affordable housing property. It is recorded against the Health and Housing capital budgets, where the approved budget is nil. The paper says: "This overspend will be resolve upon discounted resale of the property." It says the gap between the purchase price and the discounted resale price will be financed from S106 money received for the council's affordable housing scheme.

news_drafts.headline: Ribble Valley forecasts budget gaps of £0.9m in 2027/28, rising to £2.7m by 2029/30
news_drafts.lead:
Ribble Valley Borough Council set a balanced budget for 2026/27 but forecasts gaps between its planned spending and its income of £0.9m in 2027/28, £1.3m in 2028/29 and £2.7m in 2029/30. The figures are in a fees and charges report before its Community Services Committee on 20 October.

The report proposes a review of fees and charges. It would raise £8,000 more than the 3% rise in income the council has already forecast, against a gap of £0.9m in 2027/28.

A separate report on budget monitoring (the in-year check of spending against budget) covers the period to the end of August 2026. Refuse collection was £84,192 over budget, including £43,563 on temporary staff and £29,665 on agency drivers covering two vacant posts. The paper says temporary staff use has been "substantially higher" than the original budget allowed. Vehicle repairs and maintenance were £72,698 over budget, mainly from hiring replacement vehicles while others were repaired and from third-party contractor cover. A Vehicle Mechanic post has been vacant since April 2026. Diesel was £25,215 over budget. The council's finance and operations staff are analysing whether the higher staffing costs reflect a permanent change in demand.

findings.paper_title: 26-11-10 P&F Committee Report 2026-27 Q1_Q2 Corp Plan Performance v1
findings.headline: Ribble Valley reports 99.7% of invoices paid within 30 days in both Q1 and Q2 2026/27, against a 99% target
findings.detail: The paper says both quarters were rated Green. It notes the KPI is a new measure (PI FS7a) that replaces the earlier 'invoices paid on time' indicator, and gives the 2025/26 outturn as 99.3%.
findings.matters: Prompt payment performance is a supplier-relations and payment-practice measure that finance teams at other councils track on the same basis.
findings.figures: 99.7% of invoices paid within 30 days (Q1 and Q2 2026/27); target 99%; 2025/26 outturn 99.3%
findings.quote: During the first six months of 2026/2027, data for this KPI has been reported as 99.7% of invoices paid on time for both Q1 and Q2, both quarters have been RAG rated Green, as they exceed the 99% target.

findings.paper_title: 26-11-10 P&F Committee Report 2026-27 Q1_Q2 Corp Plan Performance v1
findings.headline: Ribble Valley reports 58.49% of non-domestic rates collected in the first half of 2026/27, against an annual target of 98.81%
findings.detail: The paper states the half-year figure is on track to meet the target. For 2025/26 it reports an outturn of 99.12%, which it says met and exceeded target, against a national average of 96.8%.
findings.matters: Business rates collection drives retained income under the rates retention scheme, and the national comparison lets other finance teams benchmark performance.
findings.figures: 58.49% half-year collection (Q1 and Q2 2026/27); 2026/27 target 98.81%; 2025/26 outturn 99.12%; national average 96.8%
findings.quote: For 2026/27, the half year (Q1 and Q2) percentage for non-domestic rates collected is 58.49% and is on track to meet the 98.81% target.

findings.paper_title: 26-11-10 P&F Committee Report 2026-27 Q1_Q2 Corp Plan Performance v1
findings.headline: Ribble Valley reports 58.67% of council tax collected in the first half of 2026/27, against an annual target of 99.19%
findings.detail: The paper states the half-year figure is on track to meet the target. It sets the 2025/26 annual outturn of 99.62% against a national average of 95.6%, and records that the 2025/26 target was met and rated Green.
findings.matters: Council tax collection is a core income line for a billing authority, and the paper gives a national average that peers and lenders can benchmark against.
findings.figures: 58.67% half-year collection (Q1 and Q2 2026/27); 2026/27 target 99.19%; 2025/26 outturn 99.62%; national average 95.6%
findings.quote: For 2026/27, the half year (Q1 and Q2) percentage for Council tax collected is 58.67% and is on track to meet the 99.19% target.

findings.headline: Paragraph 2.3 gives the favourable net position as £423,064, while the table and paragraph 6.1 give £423,140.
findings.detail: The same discrepancy appears in income: paragraph 2.3 gives income £484,035 above profile, while the table gives £484,111. Paragraph 4.8 gives Recovered Rent Allowances as £25,431 favourable, while the summary of major variances gives £27,128.
findings.matters: Inconsistent headline figures in a monitoring report are something a finance director or a lender would want reconciled before relying on the numbers.
findings.figures: £423,064 (paragraph 2.3) vs £423,140 (table and paragraph 6.1); £484,035 vs £484,111 income; £25,431 vs £27,128 Recovered Rent Allowances
findings.quote: Both contribute to the favourable net position of £423,064.

findings.headline: Planning application and pre-application income is £43,237 favourable at half-year, a figure the paper says fluctuates with the timing of major developments.
findings.detail: The paper says income from planning applications varies month to month and depends on whether major developments are received within the financial period. It presents the current favourable position as subject to that variation.
findings.matters: Development-driven income is volatile for all planning authorities, and the paper's caveat shows why half-year variances on it may not hold to year-end.
findings.quote: The current position shows a favourable variance of £43,237.

daily_post.headline: Income from proposed fees is not guaranteed and will depend on service usage and demand, which may change in response to price increases
daily_post.lead: Lenders and finance directors need to understand revenue projections carry demand risk. If demand falls in response to fee increases, the council will fall further short on its budget target. This is material to any assessment of financial sustainability.
